chapter: Clarence Williams's 1936 article and the dispute
title: La Rocca on Marshall Stearns, Handy and confronting Clarence Williams
summary: La Rocca recalls the 1936 broadcast, critics who opposed the ODJB's return, Stearns's admitted exaggeration, and his lawyer's confrontation of Williams over the article.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: These Negroes showed their appreciation after I had made it easy for them to come up and open his publishing concern. He didn't know me. That 20 years had passed. In 1936, Lou Gensler had a big broadcast. He tried to locate us to put us in the beginning and Benny Goodman as the end. In other words, the beginning and end. At this time, all these prophets got up in arms against us. John Hammond was one of them. He worked for Handy, I suppose, some kind of cheap lawyer or something on that order. And Handy was given out about jazz. He had given the definition of jazz to Abby Miles, what jazz music was about. He couldn't play it. They were up in arms that we were coming back to reclaim our position in the music world. This fellow, Marshall Stein, made a story about me. And he used Lloyd Kenner and Tom Brown as arch conspirators to say things that were untrue. Later on, Stein admitted to me in a letter that he only exaggerated because they didn't give the Negroes a break in this business. Can you stop the machine so I'm fine?

When I brought the band up to New York, I went to a lawyer. The lawyer told me to go over there and talk to him. And asked this Mr. Williams, did he stand behind what he mentioned in the paper. In this article, Honky Tonk to Swing. I explained to him who I was before I showed him any correspondence of the paper on or anything else. I said, do you stand behind what you say? I said, I'm going to take you to court to make you prove. There's this correction right there. Like all Negroes, when you put them on the top of a horse, they ride them to death. This Negro never would have been to New York had it been for the original Dixieland jazz band. He and all the rest of the Negroes that come from New York and New Orleans. They never would have made good unless they styled themselves on the original Dixieland recordings.
